summary: A brick tower first lit in 1904 at Crisp Point on Lake Superior; automated in 1941, decommissioned in 1992, and run as a private aid since 2012.

light.current_optic: 300 mm LED marine light (installed 2012; seasonal from 2013)

structures.type: brick, conical attached to entrance room
structures.note: 58 ft from base to lantern centre (Society's record); LighthouseFriends: fifty-eight feet tall.
Redbrick building 100 ft north of the tower for a ten-inch steam whistle; razed by 1965.
Two-story duplex 60 ft west of the tower.
Connected to the tower by a passageway; destroyed by storm in 1996; rebuilt 2006-2008.
Inland replica of the fog signal building.

staffing.note: Keepers withdrawn after the fog signal was discontinued (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Grounds always open; lighthouse and visitor center keep seasonal hours; last seven miles of Luce County Road 412 are seasonal.

stay.note: Society's home page links to volunteer keeper information. Terms not read.

facts.ownership: Luce County since 1997 (LighthouseFriends); operated by the Crisp Point Light Historical Society

aton.note: Private aid to navigation operated under a Coast Guard permit from 2012 (LighthouseFriends); Society's record: active aid.

events.note: Congress appropriated $18,000 for the station on 28 June 1902.
Station finished in June 1904; tower brick, 58 ft.
Fixed red light first exhibited on the night of 5 May 1904.
Fourth-order Fresnel lens, Sautter, Lemonnier & Cie.
Second fog-signal plant; ten-inch chime whistle.
Light changed from oil to incandescent oil vapor (Bulletin 1914, under Crisp Point).
Keepers went to help the steamer F. R. Hazard after a collision (12 June 1920).
Keeper H. P. Crittenden towed the motor boat Gladys L to shore and assisted with the Sea Fox in a gale.
Fog signal changed from steam to a six-inch siren run by diesel-driven compressed air.
Electrified and automated after two years of planning; fog signal discontinued before the last keepers were withdrawn.
Society's record: 'Year Discontinued: 1947'. LighthouseFriends ties automation to 1941; the date is unexplained.
Coast Guard razed all buildings except the tower and its attached service room.
Coast Guard decommissioned the light after the 1992 season (LighthouseFriends).
Violent storm in November destroyed the service room at the tower's base.
Transferred to Luce County (July 1997 per LighthouseFriends).
Coast Guard permit for private aid to navigation; 300 mm lens installed 23 Nov 2012; seasonal operation from 2013.

corrections.proposed: 1941 electrified and automated; 1992 decommissioned after the 1992 season; the 1947 date needs a source
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends ties the automation to 1941 and the decommissioning to after the 1992 season. The 1947 'Year Discontinued' entry in the Society's record is not explained by any source read.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The light was automated in 1941 and decommissioned after the 1992 season; a Coast Guard permit allowed seasonal operation again from 2012-2013 (LighthouseFriends; Society's record). Reports that it is lit and unlit describe different periods.

notes_for_editor:
Dates in conflict: Luce County transfer. LighthouseFriends gives July 1997; a search snippet of northernmichiganhistory.com and the Wikipedia article (not read or cited) say February 1997. The story says 1997.
Decommissioning: LighthouseFriends says the Coast Guard decommissioned the light after the 1992 season. A search snippet of the Upper Peninsula Heritage Trail page (not read) says 1993. The story uses LighthouseFriends.
Discontinuance: the Society's record gives 'Year Discontinued: 1947' and a 1947 deactivation event. LighthouseFriends ties automation to 1941 and says the fog signal ended before the last keepers left. The story states both dates and says they are unexplained. The Coast Guard Light List and any 1947 Board or Coast Guard record were not read.
Herbert P. Crittenden: the archive roster gives head keeper at Crisp Point 1917-1922; LighthouseFriends says he arrived at Crisp Point in 1921 after Gull Rock and Whitefish Point. The story uses the roster years only and avoids the arrival date.
Singleton family: LighthouseFriends prints family details and a 1925 family memory of the steamer Herman H. Hettler towing the barge Crane, with five men and a woman lost. No 1925 or 1926 Lighthouse Service Bulletin read here mentions Hettler or Crane. The memory is not used in the story. The sons are not named.
1914 launch: the Bulletin's OCR reads 'Om Endress' and 'ORA ENDRESS' in places and 'launch Endress' elsewhere. The story says the launch Endress. Check the page image before printing the full name.
Commissioner of Lighthouses 1921: cited by scan page 667 only; the printed page was not confirmed.
Lighthouse Board volume covering 1896-1897: cited by scan page 173; the printed page was not confirmed. The 1901 volume (scan 234) has the same paragraph but its OCR garbles the key phrase, so the 1897 volume is used.
The 1933 newspaper article is known only as LighthouseFriends quotes it (unnamed paper). The story cites LighthouseFriends.
Record: the characteristic 'Fl W 6s' and focal height 19.0 m are not verified. LighthouseFriends says the 1904 light was fixed red; the Society's record gives a 300 mm LED from 2012. The Light List (LLNR 7-14535) was not read. The Society's record says 'Height of light above mean high water: 58 feet' while the record's focal height is 19.0 m.
Record: visit.climbable (true) and stay (volunteer keeper programme, from the USLHS passport record) were not verified here. The Society's site confirms the volunteer keeper programme exists only as a link.
Photos: none added; not checked for licence.
Not used: Wikipedia leads (ownership 1997, status).
Fact-check 2026-10-27: the Soo Times extract begins on Bulletin PDF page 42 and the keeper's report is on page 43, so source 5 is cited as PDF pp. 42-43 (URL now #page=42). The 1988 founders are named only in their public role as founders of the Society; the story no longer gives their earlier home town. The Society's 'lease' is worded as 'got a lease' because LighthouseFriends says the lease made easier in 1994. The 1914 launch name appears in the Bulletin as 'Om Endress' and 'ORA ENDRESS'; the story keeps 'Endress' from the keeper's report, to be checked against the page image.
